newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka seeks to become tea blending centre.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka seeks to become tea blending centre.

text.p: Sri Lanka, the world's leading tea exporter, is considering allowing more tea imports in a bid to turn this Indian Ocean island into a major producer of blended teas, industry officials said on Thursday.
"We've got to expand our base for blending purposes," said Dickie Juriansz, chairman of James Finlay and Co., a big tea exporter.

"We need to allow more tea imports for blending because we're losing a major share of the market (by not doing so)," he told Reuters. "Even Sri Lankan exporters are setting up blending operations in other countries."
Outside of tea-growing countries, the beverage is usually drunk in blended form -- a mixture of teas from different origins, Juriansz said.
Sri Lanka, whose tea exports are expected to hit a record 250 million kg this calendar year, holds about 20 percent of the world tea market.

A Plantations Industries Ministry official said the government was considering easing restrictions on tea imports for a limited period with the long-term aim of making Colombo a blending centre like London and Rotterdam.
"In the global tea market, some market segments consume blends made from teas of diferent origins," he said. "To serve those markets we need to do blending."
The Tea Board now allows the import of limited quantities of teas not available in Sri Lanka, he said. Only about two million kg of tea are imported annually now.
"We will ensure that all teas that are blended will be exported," the ministry official said. "We will allow only teas above the...globally accepted quality standard for tea."

Sudath Munasinghe, director of tea at brokerage John Keells, said Sri Lanka had lost traditional markets such as Britain after heavy buying by Russia, the world's biggest tea importer, sent Ceylon tea prices soaring to record highs.
"We're losing our traditional markets purely on price," he told Reuters in an interview. "We're depending on one market. That's dangerous."
Tea brokers in London say Sri Lankan tea has almost priced itself out of a growing British market, with the daily cup now more likely to be an African blend such as Kenyan.
Sri Lankan tea exports to Britain fell 20 percent to around 5,000 tons during the first six months of 1996 while Kenya increased its share of British imports by 30 percent.
A British obsession with quick-brewing teabags, which are less suited to the large-leaf teas produced in Sri Lanka, has also hit Ceylon tea imports.
Russia and other former Soviet republics bought 40.4 million kg of Sri Lankan tea last year, up 206 percent from a year earlier, brokers Forbes and Walker said.

"Sri Lanka has the potential to become a blending centre," Munasinghe said. "Now so many people are in the tea packing business. If buyers shift packing to Dubai and Singapore we'll lose. If we find our prices go down as a result of this plan we can scrap it."
